results.content: # Significance Levels, Confidence Intervals and P-Values. Although I am slowly getting them sorted out, I still often find myself getting confused between Significance Levels, Confidence Intervals and P-Values. $\begingroup$ A p-value is the probability of obtaining a value as extreme or more extreme than the observed value when the null hypothesis is assumed. Confidence intervals are intervals that in repeated sampling would include the true parameter a certain percentage of time. The significance level is the percentage of the time that the confidence interval will not contain the parameter. Commented Jul 24, 2020 at 15:57. # Significance Levels and Confidence Intervals. Confidence intervals (only) provide a plausible range for population parameters. For instance, the population proportion would be within the range $(p\_1, p\_2)$ with 95% confidence level. And the significance level, often denoted by $\alpha$, is the complement of the confidence level only when the hypothesis testing is two sided. That is $\text{confidence level} = 1 - \text{significance level}$ in that scenario. For the one sided hypothesis testing $\text{confidence level} = 1 - 2\*\text{significance level}$. The $\text{significance level} = P(\text{Type 1 error} | H\_0 \text{true})$, and the type 1 error implies we reject the null hypothesis wrongly, then the bigger the significance level the more likely we would make a false rejection. We suppose that the null hypothesis is true and the p-value represents the probability the extreme(or more extreme) sample proportion is observed by chance: $P(\text{observed or more extreme sample statistic}|H\_0 \text{true})$. The bigger the p-value the more likely the observed sample proportion is resulted by chance and the less we would reject the null hypothesis, but the rejection depends on the significance level we set beforehand. If the p-value is smaller than the significance level we would be confident enough that the observed sample proportion is not led by chance and we would reject the null hypothesis. answered Jul 23, 2020 at 14:29. results.content:
Title: Hypothesis Testing, P Values, Confidence Intervals, and Significance in Research - DoveMed
Hypothesis Testing, P Values, Confidence Intervals, and Significance in Research. # Hypothesis Testing, P Values, Confidence Intervals, and Significance in Research. Hypothesis testing, P values, confidence intervals, and significance are fundamental concepts in research and statistical analysis. This comprehensive article aims to provide a clear understanding of hypothesis testing, P values, confidence intervals, and significance, highlighting their importance in research and their interpretation. * Selecting a significance level: The significance level (α) determines the threshold for rejecting the null hypothesis. * Collecting and analyzing data: Data is collected and analyzed using appropriate statistical tests to determine the likelihood of observing the observed effect if the null hypothesis is true. * Interpreting the results: The test statistic and its associated P value are used to make a decision regarding the rejection or acceptance of the null hypothesis. P values are a measure of the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis. * Interpreting P values: A P value less than the chosen significance level (α) suggests evidence to reject the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis. A P value greater than α suggests weak evidence against the null hypothesis. * P value thresholds: The significance level (α) determines the threshold for rejecting the null hypothesis. * P value limitations: P values alone do not provide information about the effect size or the clinical significance of the findings. * Relationship with P values: If the null hypothesis value is outside the confidence interval, it provides evidence against the null hypothesis. Significance refers to the statistical conclusion regarding the rejection or acceptance of the null hypothesis based on the chosen significance level and P value. * Statistical significance: Statistical significance is determined by comparing the P value to the significance level (α). If the P value is less than α, the result is statistically significant. Hypothesis testing, P values, confidence intervals, and significance are essential components of statistical analysis in research. Understanding these concepts enables researchers to draw meaningful conclusions, make informed decisions, and communicate the significance of their findings. # Related Articles.
